comments.text:
"How do they know what snake it is?"

Australian here who is familiar with snakes: Hospitals here have lab kits called SVDKs that can detect which venom is present with a swab. Not sure why they didn't use it in this case. It's one of the many reasons we're taught not to wash snake bites or try to "suck" the venom out: they want to keep some venom close to the bite site for later identification.

I'm a little surprised they didn't hold off on the Tiger antivenom until they could identify the snake though - I believe it's a relatively slow-acting venom. Her own first aid sounded pretty ad-hoc, but you can see the paramedic has applied a bite kit.

I'm a trail runner and run in Red Belly, Tiger and Eastern Brown territories, so usually carry a bite kit with me. A bad Eastern Brown bite can kill in under 30 minutes without first aid. A timely and correctly applied bite kit extends that to more like 9-12 hours. Good first aid really does make a massive difference with snakes here.
comments.author: @msmyrk

comments.text: I will say: putting a tourniquet on a snake bite is not a good idea in most of the world. It's only considered procedure in Australia because Australia doesn't have any vipers- which is a family of snakes that have hemotoxic and myotoxic venom, aka it attacks your blood and muscles. Australia's venomous snakes are all elapids, which have neurotoxic venom, so the damage can be localized by a tourniquet.

comments.text: So with "Asthma panic attack", from my own experience growing up with severe asthma, my guess is that it probably means they're having an asthmatic episode and beginning to panic about it.. I learned very early on that if you start to panic during an asthma attack, you're only going to make it so much worse because your heart rate increases, your need for oxygen increases as a result, you begin to experience air hunger, and things rapidly start to go downhill.. Learning to control your panic response is crucial if you're a chronic asthmatic! Slow, deep breaths and remaining as calm as possible are the things that can save your life, even if it feels like you're breathing through one of those "coffee stirrer" straws with the two super tiny holes. Do that until you can get the help you need! (I'm not a doctor, and I was not taught this information anywhere, I just gathered it from my own life experience of struggling to breathe, use this information at your own risk)
